sentences.text: The dull explanation is right and Ari has known it since he was about fourteen.
Arctic foxes cache.
It is one of the most thoroughly documented things they do.

A fox on a seabird cliff will take and bury hundreds of eggs in a season — there is a study from Wrangel Island with a number over nine hundred — and they bury them one at a time, in scattered places, and they remember where.
They cache anything that might be worth having later.
In a hard winter a cached egg from July is the difference.
The behaviour is not fussy about what the thing is; it is triggered by *surplus*, and a fox that finds something it cannot use now and might use later will take it and put it somewhere.
Wool smells of sheep and of people and of lanolin, which is to say it smells strongly of something that was recently alive.
And a fox does not have a category for *glove*.
It has a category for *smells of animal, portable, not currently useful*, and a hand-knitted mitten off a windowsill fits that description exactly and so does an egg.
That is the whole of it.
There is no puzzle.
Every wildlife biologist Ari has ever mentioned it to has said essentially the same four sentences, cheerfully, and one of them said it was a nice example and asked for photographs.
What none of them accounted for, and what Ari has stopped raising because it makes him sound like a person with a theory, is the sorting.
And the fact that in twelve years and something over three hundred items, not one thing that was not warm has ever been in that cache.
No plastic.
No paper.
No rope, and there is rope all over that farm.
No leather that had not been lined.
He has tested it, which he thinks is the only genuinely scientific thing he has ever done.
At fifteen he put four objects out on the wall by the byre on the same evening, all about the same size and weight: a woollen sock, a nylon sock, a strip of tarpaulin, and a length of baler twine.
The woollen sock went that night.
The other three were on the wall a week later and he brought them in.
He did it again the following spring with the same result and a fifth object, a fleece hat, which also went.
That is a sample of two trials and he is aware that this would not get past anybody.
